speakeroldname: Hon. IAN MACKENZIE (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: SINGLE UNEMPLOYED MEN IN OTTAWA-QUESTION AS TO ACTION BY FEDERAL GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
This is the fourth occasion upon which I have had the honour to present to the house through the committee of supply the estimates of the Department of National Defence. It has been more or less a recognized custom for the last two or three sessions that, before the committee enters upon the discussion in detail of the various items, a presentation be made in a general way with reference to the defence policy and the general purpose of the estimates.
At the outset I must ask the indulgence of hon. members if I review in some detail the situation with reference to national defence. I can only hope that the presentation of essential facts and figures with reference to the past, an analysis of the situation with reference to the present, and a pronouncement of policy with reference to the future, may be of some assistance to hon. members in contributing to a fair and informed discussion of one of our greatest national problems, that of national defence. However, before I come to a discussion of the estimates themselves I should like to consider certain declarations of policy which have been made previously in the house during the present session. I do this not in any controversial sense but simply in order to set up a background for what I propose to say.
The government's policy in regard to national defence has been stated repeatedly in this house by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and by other ministers. It is, I think, fair to characterize it as a rational policy of national defence. In connection with its estimates it is the duty of the Department of National Defence not so much to lay down a policy in regard to our relationship with other nations as to provide an effective instrument for upholding the policy of the government in the eventuality of the utilization of force becoming necessary. In other words, the function of the department over which I preside is not to lay down policy but to provide an instrument for carrying it out.
Authoritative statements of the government's policy have already been made to the house this session by the Prime Minister and the
Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). It is not necessary at this time that I review the broad underlying philosophy on which the policies enunciated are based; but it may be valuable, in considering the concrete task of defence, to mention once again one or two passages from the remarks of two distinguished leaders of the government, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice. An excellent contribution also was made to the discussion by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion).
On March 30, 1939, the Prime Minister said, as reported on page 2423 of Hansard:
... it is for the government to recommend and for parliament to decide upon the course to follow.
Again:
. . . When for any reason there is cause to believe that one or more nations are determined upon aggression, and may have in mind domination of other countries by force, it may be that enemy, not the parliament of this country or even its people, who will decide whether it best serves its purpose to regard Canada as liable to attack in any conflict in which it may be engaged with any other part of the British Commonwealth of Nations.
Again at page 2426:
We would not go into a war merely because of legal uncertainty as to our power to stay out. We would not stay out of a war merely because we had provided unquestioned technical freedom to do so. Our country's decisions on such vital matters, now or later, will depend on deeper forces, they will depend on the thoughts and feelings of our people. . . .
. . . it is desirable nevertheless to consider some questions which would arise in the event of our participation in such a conflict. That participation could not be passive or formal, nor could it be unplanned or irresponsible. It will be necessary to consider in consultation with others involved and with regard to the objectives and operations of the enemy, what would be the most effective form our action and our cooperation could take.
Without quoting textually I would ask the house to recall the Prime Minister's observations as to the improbability of an expeditionary force, his pledge that conscription for such a purpose will not be adopted, his analysis of the great changes effected by a shifting of the balance of power and scientific invention. But there is one passage towards the conclusion of the Prime Minister's remarks on the subject of defence in relation to foreign policy which I wish to quote with emphasis. It is found on page 2426 of Hansard:
The heaping up of rival armaments, the clash of new doctrines, the concentration of power in a few hands, are factors which make it necessary to become prepared for whatever may happen. It is not possible to ignore that situation.
Again, having regard to the practical problem of defence which confronts my department, it is important to recall some observa-
Supply-National Defence

tions made by the Minister of Justice. My colleague from the province of Quebec effectively dissipated the myth of neutrality in any vital war where British and Canadian interests were concerned, with a reasoned analysis of the implications of such a theory. He quoted Oppenheim's definition of neutrality :
Neutrality may be defined as the attitude of impartiality adopted by a third state towards belligerents and recognized by belligerents, such attitude creating rights and duties between the impartial state and the belligerents.
And he said:
Can such an attitude of impartiality be possible in Canada during a war in our present international situation? A neutral state, as I said, would have to intern British troops or war vessels. I ask any one of my fellow countrymen whether they believe seriously that this could be done without a civil war in Canada. A neutral state would have to possess forces sufficient to deter any belligerent power from violating these neutrality rights which Canada would have to uphold even against Britain if it were neutral.
And later:
... if any dictator in the world has made up his mind that the British Commonwealth is going to be disrupted he is basing his future projects on utter fallacy.
With regard to Canada's direct defence responsibilities and the manner in which they should be honoured, let me quote again from the Minister of Justice as reported at page 2469 of Hansard:
There is no reason on earth why pious aspirations, unsupported by anything more substantial, should be more effective protection for us than they proved to be for Abyssinia or China; and we must remember that even the excellent Czech army proved inadequate when left without support. . . .
We cannot lull ourselves into a false security simply by making fine speeches, uttering great sentiments on the beauty of having no military expenditures, and being strong for peace.
Then, after pointing out that even if Canada were neutral or independent she would need security and would have to seek it by alliances with Great Britain and the United States, the Minister of Justice went on to point out the urgent necessity-
. . . in the interests of Canada that there should be a full understanding between Britain and the United States, and cooperation in coastal defence on the Pacific. But again I say, is not the British sea power an asset to be preserved in our own sacred Canadian interests?
These citations from these authoritative utterances of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice indicate very clearly the nature of the task which governmental policy has placed in the hands of the Department of National Defence, and it will be my duty this afternoon to describe to this committee the
[Mr. I. Mackenzie.!
manner in which the Department of National Defence in recent years has endeavoured to carry out that task. I desire to amplify the statements of policy submitted to the house during the present session by former declarations of policy, so as to indicate to my colleagues in this chamber the continuity of policy which has existed both in regard to our foreign relations and in regard to the necessity for making adequate provision for national security in the Dominion of Canada.
Almost immediately after taking office in October 1935 the present government decided to strengthen Canada's national defences. Three main reasons impelled this decision. The first one was the disturbed international situation in both Europe and Asia; the second, the technical advice that modern invention and change in technique of warfare had brought out new kinds and degrees of vulnerability for Canada; the third, an appreciation of the depleted condition of the country's defence equipment.
The decision to strengthen our defences, made in 1935 and actively pursued during the past three years, was set out in progressive declarations of government policy, through imperial conference resolutions and in formal pronouncements by the Prime Minister on various occasions. I refer first to the declaration made by the imperial conference of 1923:
The primary responsibility of each portion of the empire was for its own local defence.
And again:
Neither Great Britain nor the dominions could be committed to the extent of any active obligation except with the definite assent of their own governments.
Speaking in this house on March 10, 1936, as reported at pages 922 and 923 of Hansard, the Prime Minister said:
-we have made clear at various conferences that any action in -the nature of military obligations of any sort would be entered into by the government of the day only after such bad been recommended to parliament by the government and approved by parliament itself.
Then on February 13, 1937, as appears at page 1050 of Hansard, the Prime Minister stated:
By all means, let us make the most of our friendship with the United States. By all means, let us make the most of our friendship and kinship with Great Britain and with every other part of the British empire. By all means let us continue to be friends with every other nation, because in that direction, more perhaps than in any other, security lies. But let us realize that unless we do something to help ourselves these countries cannot .be expected to help at a time of world crisis, or great peril. ... So far as the Monroe doctrine is concerned, may I ask this house whether.

Supply-National Defence
having regard to our relations with the United States and our desire to maintain the friendliest possible relations with that country, we are prepared to surrender to that country the whole of our obligation in the matter of protection against foreign aggression? Is it likely that we shall be able to maintain friendly relations with the United States if we do nothing to defend our own coasts but simply take the attitude that we shall look to them for our defence? Similarly with regard to England. Are members of this government who are to represent Canada at the imperial conference to be asked to assert Canada's equality of status with all the nations of the British commonwealth and at the same time to tell the British government -that we are relying upon Great Britain to protect our coasts and will do nothing to help ourselves because we have their protection?
Then the Prime Minister continued:
I submit that sponging by a nation is, in the eyes of other nations, exactly the same as it is in the case of individuals .	.	. anynation that does not wish to become a belligerent in a war must at least be able to see that the waters -adjacent to its own co-asts are so patrolled by its own vessels that no belligerent can come and operate from that base against some other country with which it may be at war. .	.	.
There will be no participation by Canada in a war overseas except by the consent of our own parliament. ... I say that while we are doing what we are doing for Canada we believe that in this way we can make the most effective contribution towards -the security of all countries that may have like institutions, like ideals, -and principles of freedom similar to our own.
Next I come to the finding of the imperial conference of 1937, which has a definite bearing on the situation:
.	.	. the conference found general agreement among its members that the security of each of their countries can be increased by cooperation in such matters -as the free interchange of information concerning the state of their naval, military and air forces, the continuance of the arrangements already initiated by some of them for concerting the scale of the defences of ports, and measures for cooperation in the defence of communications and other common interests. At the same time the conference recognized that it is the sole responsibility of the several parliaments of the British commonwealth to decide the nature and scope of their own defence policy.
Next, Mr. Chairman, comes that famous declaration, already quoted in this house, by the president of the United States on August 18, 1938:
The Dominion of Canada is part of the sisterhood of the British empire. I give to you assurance that the people of the United States will not stand idly by if domination of Canadian soil is -threatened by any other empire.
On August 21, 1938, the Prime Minister of Canada commented upon that statement as follows:
The people of Canada deeply appreciate all that is implied by the president's visit. At the same time they know they have their own
responsibilities for maintaining Canadian soil as -a homeland for free men in -the western hemisphere .	.	. they will be quick to see
that the assurance given by the president has, if anything, increased rather than lessened our responsibilities.
We, too, have our obligations as a good friendly neighbour, and one of them is to see that, at our own instance, our country is made as immune from attack or possible invasion as we oan reasonably be expected to make it, and that, should the occasion ever arise, enemy forces should not be able to pursue their way, either by land, sea or air to the United States, across Canadian territory.
That brings me, sir, to a consideration, of the functions of national defence in the Dominion of Canada, and I suggest to hon. gentlemen that in determining from year to year what shall be the program of the department it is necessary to appraise, in the first place, the relevant aspects of the dominion's policy with regard to external affairs; in the second place, the nature and extent of the risks to lie apprehended, and, in the third place the types of weapons and equipment and the amount of force required for the purpose of coping with such risks.
It is submitted now that the program adopted and pursued during the past three years, and still under active development, is strictly in accordance with the country's external affairs policy. The department has proceeded on two major assumptions, the first being that Canada will not be engaged in any war against the United States of America, and the second that Canada will not be engaged single-handed in any war against an overseas power, and that any war in -which Canada may become engaged will be in association with other great powers whom she will be supporting and by whom she will be supported, for the protection of vital and essential principles. These two major assumptions, Mr. Chairman, limit the scale of the preparations necessary. In the first place, we do not have to fortify our southern border. In the second place, the extent of defence on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts need not be on such a scale as to cope with a major attack or attempted invasion.
A third important consideration which vitally affects the character and extent of the program imposed upon the Department of National Defence is the nature of this country's economy. I desire to say a word about our national trade. I believe Canada is now the fourth trading nation in the -world. With respect to other vital aspects of our economy she is dependent upon external trade. Our trade with the United States, being mostly overland, is relatively immune from hostile interference. This represents only half our
Supply-National Defence

external trade. The other half is carried entirely by sea, forty per cent to the sister nations of the commonwealth and about ten per cent to foreign countries.
Without discussing at the moment considerations of policy, and viewing the matter only from a technical military standpoint, it is to be assumed that an enemy at war with Great Britain would endeavour to cut off trade between the British Isles and our own dominion. It is a very large question, not to be omitted from military consideration, whether Canada's economic life could be maintained without that 1750,000,000 of export and import trade. The department must therefore be prepared to defend our seaports, our terminals, our coastal shipping and the focal areas of our offshore trade in the vicinity of our seaports from probable interference or attack.
Possibly this might be the appropriate moment- to review briefly the historic evolution of Canada's defence problem. Our early settlements along the St. Lawrence lived for almost two centuries under the constant menace of attack, in the early days from the Indians and later from the colonies to the south. It was in those days that Canada's unique militia system had its birth. Every ablebodied man was subject to the call to arms for the defence of his home and his community. The basis of organization was the town company, for the direction of which the local seigneur or the chief citizen was responsible to the governor. In the days of the American revolution, and for years afterwards, there was constant fear of attack from *the south. The English settlers, including the United Empire Loyalists, banded themselves together in New Brunswick and Upper Canada in county regiments; every ablebodied man was required to attend at least one annual muster.
Gradually, Mr. Chairman, the militia became formalized into definite units, but the history of many of the outstanding militia regiments of to-day can be traced back without a break to the very beginning of our Canadian history. And the much discussed universal service clause in our present Militia Act is the oldest law in Canada, dating back to the earliest French settlements in Quebec.
For two centuries of Canada's history she lived in constant peril of attack and a strong militia was vital and essential for her safety. Then, in that century between 1814 and 1914 there was the celebrated hundred years of peace. Steady development of friendly relationships with our kin across the border resulted in such a close affinity that the very

thought of possibility of war was dismissed from our minds. A friendly United States on the south, wide seas upon our eastern and western flanks, and frozen fastnesses to the north developed in Canada a sense of security which amounted almost to an obsession of immunity from attack.
There was for a time justification for that feeling of immunity. It rested, however, upon one factor which has not yet been mentioned, namely, the British navy. In the days when British fleets patrolled and dominated the seven seas, we, in Canada, were indeed immune from attack.
There was no lack in Canada of recognition of the great service performed by the British navy. Until very recent years Canada did not feel herself impelled to make any contribution to naval defence, but we did maintain our militia institutions. We drew on our militia to support Great Britain in the South African war, and we threw the whole weight of Canada's man power and the whole of our national effort into the great and tragic European war of twenty years ago.
The significance of this brief historical review is that since the dawn of our history in Canada the essential defence problem of successive Canadian governments has been the maintenance of our militia institutions. Both in the days of the Indian wars and in the days of immunity which came after, the militia was the effective instrument for coping with our military responsibility. According to some of our best thinkers, those days have gone forever. We face a new problem at the present time. A fleet on the surface of the seas is no longer a sure defence against hostile attack. The submarine can go under and the aircraft over those walls of steel. Not long ago-in fact only a few months ago- intrepid air men took off in Russia, flew across the Arctic wastes and all across Canada without a single stop, landing in California. Only a few months ago a squadron of the British Royal Air Force flew from Egypt to Australia, a distance greater than from the heart of Europe to Montreal, and back again.
In other words, it is to-day possible for hostile aircraft to take off in mid Europe, fly to Canada, drop their bombs and fly back again without landing. Even in the last war, as we all know, submarines operated off the Atlantic coast of North America with devastating effect. So that after a century of immunity from attack Canada is to-day again vulnerable to enemy hostilities and has to cope with a real problem of national defence, just as she did in the early centuries of her history.

Supply-National Defence
This brings me to a consideration of Canada's defence program, upon which we have embarked, after very carefully weighing the foregoing factors. It is now considered by those who are qualified and competent to advise that in the event of great international conflict Canada must be prepared in the first place to maintain a ceaseless patrol of all possible lines of approach from which attack may come, and have in readiness at the right place forces and weapons adequate to cope with attacks of the type and scale to be apprehended.
In the second place she must defend her territory from raiding attack from submarine, aircraft or other craft which may successfully escape blockade and seek to inflict damage upon Canadian property, especially that utilized for transportation and industrial production.
In the third place, she must defend her seaports, terminals, and shipping and overseas trade from attack or interceptions by belligerents.
In the fourth place she must prevent the utilization by belligerents of her territory or territorial waters, of the myriad bays and coves on her deeply indented coast line, and of the air over her territory, for the purpose of or in the course of attacks upon any other friendly or allied nation.
For these purposes which I have specified, the conclusion has been reached-although in regard to that conclusion there are differences of opinion-that the first line of defence for the Dominion of Canada must be the air force. The navy must be strengthened, and the militia must be properly safeguarded.
In 1935 and 1936, in anticipation of possible repercussions from the impending conflict in the far east it was considered the greatest risk in Canada was on the Pacific coast. Accordingly in preparing our defences the department laid down the following priorities as a guide:
1.	Fortification of Pacific coast prior to Atlantic coast.
2.	Development of the air force in priority to navy and, so far as possible, the navy in priority to the militia.
3.	Reorganizing and re-equiping the militia as soon as our resources permit us to do so.
That plan has been followed to the utmost extent practicable.
The task confronting this government in 1936 was a very formidable task indeed.
It is my intention this afternoon not to condemn and certainly not to criticize, but to explain what had to be done in the last three years, and to submit to members of the
committee an exact picture of the situation of our national defence in Canada when I assumed the responsibility of my office in 1935.
On taking office in October I immediately called for reports from the heads of the three services in the Department of National Defence as to the state of departmental organization in relation to the tasks confronting it. A most serious state of deficiency in equipment was revealed.| The government immediately decided upon a policy of strengthening the national defences. As hon. members may recall, the Prime Minister stated in the house in 1937 that for very grave reasons of national policy which, in retrospect, hon. members will appreciate, it was decided to make no major effort in 1936, although in fact there was a substantial increase in the defence appropriation for that year. And a beginning at least was made in repairing certain deficiencies. This afforded time for a very careful study of the whole problem, and in 1937 the government laid its policy fully before the house in connection with major increases in appropriations. At that time and more briefly last year I laid before hon. members some of the information as to the state of the various services brought to my notice in the reports of the heads of the three services received shortly after taking office in 1935.
In regard to our naval service the report I received was as follows, that even assuming effective air force and militia cooperation Canada did not possess adequate naval forces to guarantee neutrality of Canada in a war in which she did not wish to be a belligerent. Assuming that at a particular time the danger would exist on only one coast the minimum force adequate to maintain an effective naval patrol would be, on one coast, six torpedo boat destroyers, four mine sweepers and twelve auxiliary vessels. In October, 1935, Canada possessed two effective torpedo boat destroyers, two torpedo boat destroyers due for retirement, and one inefficient mine sweeper.
Then, it was reported that the barracks, dockyards and other shore facilities of the naval forces were generally antiquated and inadequate. The naval magazine at Esquimalt harbour was condemned as far back as 1905, and the wireless equipment at both Halifax and Esquimalt was inadequate.
In regard to our military services the report was that there was not a single modern antiaircraft gun in Canada. The stock of field gun ammunition on hand represented ninety minutes fired at normal rates for the field guns inherited from the great war. The stock
Supply-National Defence

in Canada was less than one-half of the equipment ammunition which travels with the guns, and there were no reserves. Existing field artillery was unsuitable for mechanical traction and outranged by modern guns to the extent of 3,000 to 6,000 yards. Coast defence armaments were obsolescent and in many cases defective. Firing practice had been restricted in order to prolong life of guns.
Beyond a few tractors for guns of the permanent force batteries, no provision had been made for mechanical transport for defence purposes. Canada possessed no tanks or service armoured cars and no tractors for heavy and field equipment. In regard to anti-gas defence, it was reported that there was an insufficient supply of respirators for even the permanent force suitable for training only, and none available for mobilization. No steps had been taken to organize other forms of anti-gas defence.

There were no aero engines manufactured in Canada, and the development of an aero engine industry to the point of production would take two years. As already indicated, approximately $2,000.000 has been expended as initial or progress payments on items ordered, but not yet delivered, and with respect to which the total commitment -will be approximately $12,000,000. Chief among these items are the following: For coast defence armament: high angle mountings for heavy coast guns; a number of medium coast defence guns and mountings; a number of guns for anti-motor torpedo boat action, to be situated at certain harbours for close-in defence against small craft which may elude outer defences; relining of additional heavy guns in England; fire control equipment for coast defence batteries, ordered from the war office; communication equipment for coast defence batteries, ordered in Canada; 130 search light equipments for anti-aircraft defence. The arrangement for the production of this equipment in Canada involved extended negotiations with the industry, since this is a product which had never before been produced in Canada. It was finally found possible to obtain competitive bids.

Supply-National Defence
In regard to coast defence ammunition, while it is not considered to be in the public interest to give too much detail regarding armament and ammunition orders, there has been ordered from the old country additional coast defence ammunition to the amount of $842,266. This includes the various types of ammunition for the coast defence guns, some of which are purchased in the complete rounds; in other cases the components are purchased separately and assembled in our own arsenals. Also in some cases we buy certain components from the old country and produce certain components ourselves.
As to anti-aircraft equipment, answering the question of my hon. friend a few moments ago, they were ordered by the previous administration and since then there have been ordered fourteen anti-aircraft guns of the 4-5 inch calibre and four of 3-inch calibre for future delivery, at an estimated total cost of $1,289,240.

The barrack area generally has also been improved and roads and services extended.

At London, Ontario, mechanical transport garage for the Royal Canadian Army Service Corps was constructed at Wolsley barracks.

At London, Ontario, a small arms munition magazine was constructed.

At Valcartier, six magazines were constructed out of funds provided in the vote for engineer services and works, for use in connection with the Dominion arsenal.

With reference to training, the appropriation for permanent force training in 1935-36 was 8113,850. By a series of small annual increases this was brought up to 8168,850 for the current year. Considering the 1935 appropriation as an irreducible minimum, the department has had in the three years, over and above the irreducible minimum, 8101,000 for additional training over and above that for 1935-36. These additional funds were used in 1936-37 for the provision of courses of training abroad, and in 1937-38 for additional courses abroad in coast defence, anti-aircraft defence and tank training, and for the mobilization of the Royal Canadian Horse Artillery Brigade at Petawawa, and training of the Royal Canadian Dragoons, as a regiment for one month at Petawawa.
In 1938-39, for the first time in many years all permanent force units were concentrated at Camp Borden for manoeuvres, affording commanders an opportunity to practise leadership in the field. The newly formed antiaircraft battery, Royal Canadian Artillery, was also given training in a practice camp near Trenton.
Por the non-permanent force, the appropriation for training of the militia in 1935-36 was $1,588,800. There was no increase in 1936-37, but fairly substantial increases were made in the following two years, so that the appropriation in 1938-39 was $2,035,800. Treating the appropriations of 1935 and 1936 as an irreducible minimum, the increases of the past two years have given the non-permanent militia $447,000 for training over and above that which was possible on the 1935 appropriation. In 1936-37, although there was no increase in funds, certain technical arms were given slightly longer training periods. In
1937-38 an additional 5,000 men were trained in camps and fortifications. The number of officers and men attending schools of instruction was increased over the previous year by 1,468. Additional expense was incurred in the technical training of units reorganized along mechanical lines.
In 1938-39 there were further increases in the periods of annual training and in the number permitted to train, an increase in the number training in camp, by 12,700.
Coast defence units, especially the newly formed units at Vancouver, Sydney and Saint John, were given additional training.
I now come to the question of the industrial survey. In 1936-37 a master-general of the
ordnance was reappointed and under his chairmanship there was formed the navy, army and air supply committee. During the past two years this committee has made a thorough survey of industrial firms and plants, with a view to ascertaining, tabulating and indexing the available industrial resources of the country for the production of military requirements at a time of emergency. More than 1,500 firms have been surveyed and the information obtained has been tabulated and indexed in convenient form for reference.
This is the first time in Canadian history that peace time provision has been made, on a scientific basis, for the mobilization of industry, should the necessity arise. Largely as a result of the work of the master-general of the ordnance and the supply committee many of our requirements, not hitherto obtainable in Canada, are now being produced for the department in this country. The development of domestic sources of supply for the greatest possible variety of our requirements, is one of the most valuable contributions to our national defence potential that could be made.

The Royal Canadian Navy will be increased by 21 officers, and 363 ratings, as follows:

It is hoped by this increase to provide trained personnel in anticipation of new vessels to be acquired in the future. In an
emergency, it is possible to acquire vessels for various purposes very quickly, but if these are to be manned by trained naval personnel, it is necessary that a nucleus, in excess of the complement of the existing ships, shall be trained in advance.
In regard to the Royal Canadian Volunteer Reserve, it is proposed to add two new divisions to that force during the coming year. The sixteen present divisions are located at the following points: Halifax, Charlottetown, Saint John, Quebec, Montreal, Ottawa, Toronto, Hamilton, Winnipeg, Regina, Saskatoon, Edmonton, Calgary, Vancouver, Prince Rupert, Port Arthur.
Supply-National Defence

It is expected that one of the two new divisions will be situated in Montreal, for French-speaking boys. The existing Montreal unit is for those who speak English. There is keen competition among several cities for the other proposed new division, and its location will be determined by the prospects for the quickest and most efficient recruitment up to strength.
Then, the Royal Canadian Naval Reserve exists for the purpose of adding to the resources of the naval forces, officers and men of the mercantile marine. The Royal Canadian Naval Reserve has an authorized complement of 500, and its actual strength is only a little more than half the authorization. No increase in establishment is contemplated, therefore, but every effort will be made to add to the strength of the reserve during the coming year.
In regard to the Fishermen's Reserve I would say that great success was experienced in organizing that reserve on the Pacific coast, with a strength of 40 skippers and 160 seamen. It is now proposed to establish a similar reserve on the Atlantic coast, of equal strength with that on the Pacific. All 400 of the personnel of the Fishermen's Reserve will be given thirty days' training.
A new unit is being added to the naval reserve this year, to be known as the Royal Canadian Fleet Reserve. This corps will be recruited from men discharged from the Royal Canadian Navy. Upon discharge from the Royal Canadian Navy, pensioners and those who have served less than the full time to qualify for pension will be given the opportunity to enlist in the Royal Canadian Fleet Reserve for a period of five years. Ratings will be trained in the second and fourth years of each period of enrolment. The object of the fleet reserve is to retain as available naval ratings who have already received training in the Royal Canadian Navy.
In regard to ships, it is proposed during the coming year to add one major unit to the floating establishment of the Royal Canadian Navy. One flotilla leader is to be purchased at an estimated price of $820,000. This vessel will be purchased from the admiralty. A ship, built at the same time as the four destroyers recently purchased, is understood to be available. Acquisition of a leader, whose interior arrangements are adapted for the accommodation of staff, will make it possible for the destroyer flotillas to be trained in flotilla manoeuvres, and will give to Canadian staff officers experience in the direction of such activities.
In addition, it is proposed, during the coming year, to draw up complete working plans for the building in Canada of anti-submarine

vessels, motor torpedo boats, and a training schooner for the west coast.
It is believed, from the success of Canadian shipyards in building the four mine sweepers now in commission, that Canada has the capacity to produce both these additional types of naval craft. The requirements of Canadian defence contemplate the use of such vessels. Motor torpedo boats, it is believed, will be especially useful on the river St. Lawrence. Construction of another training schooner for use on the Pacific will give the same facilities for training on that coast as have been successfully established on the Atlantic in H.M.C.S. Venture. Some minor yard craft such as ammunition lighters, motorboats, et cetera, will be built for use in naval harbours during 1939-40.
New construction works during the coming year will involve the expenditure of $358,500 at Halifax and $545,800 at Esquimalt. A new barrack wing, a new torpedo depot and numerous additions to the Bedford magazine will be provided on the east coast. On the west coast there will be an extension to the dockyard wharves, various storehouses, some small additions to the barrack blocks, and a number of additional units for the Esquimalt magazine.
Then, in regard to naval stores, may I say that the vote for naval stores has been doubled. The greatest increase is for the acquisition of armament stores, such as guns, ammunition, torpedoes, depth charges, and so on. The expenditure on armament stores during 1939-40 will be $729,000 as against $117,767 last year. Miscellaneous stores for ships and harbour defence purposes, to be acquired during the coming year, will include additional antisubmarine and anti-torpedo nets for both east and west coasts.
I now come to the militia services. For the militia services in the year 1939-40 the department asks $20,775,600, whereas in 1938-39 it asked $16,727,020, representing an increase of $4,048,580. This entire increase is being utilized in the acquisition of stores and equipment-chiefly armament stores. Training of the permanent and non-permanent militia is being maintained at the increased level arrived at by steady progress during the past three years. In the non-permanent militia, fortress troops will receive twenty-one days' training, other technical arms twelve, thirteen and fourteen days' training; and the minimum number of days for any branch of the service will be eleven days.
The total estimates for general stores in the present year amount to $8,836,793 as compared with $4,384,437 in the year 1938-39, or an increase of $4,452,356. Salaries, pay and allowances, operating expenses generally, will consume approximately $1,400,000 of this, and

Supply-National Defence
the sum available for the actual purchase of military stores and equipment will be $7,486,190.
As already explained, there have been placed during the past two years orders for various supplies which have not yet been delivered. Deliveries during 1939-40 are expected to use up, of this year's appropriation, the sum of $3,773,000. This is not the full cost of pending future deliveries, but covers progress results expected to be achieved during the current fiscal year, and for which it is necessary that funds be provided in this year's appropriations.
One of the most important steps to be taken this year is a commencement of the provision of new clothing for the non-permanent militia. For twenty years the nonpermanent militia has been struggling along with clothing left over from the war. Militia officers report that not only has recruiting been adversely affected by the unattractive, old. worn-out uniforms used by the non-permanent militia on parade, but that the turnover, even in some of the most popular units, has been most discouraging. In some units the annual turnover has been in excess of fifty per cent.
On this basis, effective training and the development of experienced personnel for defence has been made almost impossible. During the coming year we intend to buy
20,000	new jackets and 10,000 pairs of trousers, as a first measure towards the reclothing of the non-permanent militia in better fitting garments of smarter appearance. Khaki will be adhered to. In addition to the normal replacement and other incidental clothing expenses, this provision of new jackets and trousers is expected to cost $174,250. The full increase in the appropriation for clothing and miscellaneous stores is more than $500,000, largely due to the necessity of furnishing the non-permanent militia with more complete and better equipment. For instance, the assembling of larger formations in central training camps requires increased quantities of camp equipment. In addition to the above it is expected by supplementary estimate that provision will be made for boots for the non-permanent militia during the present year.
In connection with the question of armaments and ammunition, the amount asked for armament stores in 1939-40 is $4,299,371. Of this, the sum required to meet payments on past orders expected to mature during the year is $3,323,076. This leaves for initiating new purchases of armaments only $976,295.
The amount asked for 1939-40 for ammunition procurement is $2,499,158. Of this, the sum required to meet payments on past orders ready for delivery during the year is $408,303.
This leaves for new spending in 1939^40 on ammunition $2,090,855. The figures with regard to ammunition include operation of the dominion arsenals at Quebec and Val-cartier, as well as the development of production in private industrial channels in Canada and the procurement from England of such items as cannot be obtained within the dominion.
The provision for signal equipment is $388,400. This is a substantial increase over last year, and allows for the procurement of mechanically propelled vehicles, wireless and radio equipment and general training equipment. Out of the $128,000 provided for mechanical and water transport there will be acquired two war office pattern ambulances, six motorcycles, one motorboat for Halifax, and the replacement of old cars and trucks.
There has been provided approximately $103,600 for the continuous operation of an important unit of the Lindsay arsenal throughout the year. This plant will be used in connection with the production of cartridge cases. Operations are now ready to begin, if they have not begun within the past few days.
Then in connection with future delivery, the major items for which orders will be placed in 1939-40. but with respect to which only partial payments will be required, are as follows:
Provision and development of mechanically propelled vehicles, $426,800.
Bren gun accessories such as chests, tripods, ammunition fillers, etc., $1,192,400.
Searchlight and sound locators, $400,000.
Communication equipment for eastern fortresses, $477,000.
It has already been explained that with regard to most of the important items in the way of armament stores, the time required for production is such that delivery seldom takes place in the year in which the order is placed. In some instances five years will be required to complete contracts already let. This makes it necessary to obtain from parliament authority to enter into contracts for which in that year little or no funds will be required. Sometimes only a small partial vote is asked for in order that authority may be obtained to proceed with negotiations.
There are other requirements urgently needed in connection with which the problem has not been solved as to how they are to be procured. They are not manufactured in Canada. The requirement is so small that the overhead cost of setting up a special plant seems prohibitive. They are made in Great Britain, but the British rearmament program demands the entire output. It has just been mentioned that the department will have approximately $3,000,000 this year for initiating new purchases of arms and ammunition.
Supply-National Defence

A great deal of this will be utilized in the operation of our own arsenals and in purchasing relatively simple items that can be produced by Canadian industry. But where new items are to be ordered, the actual disbursement during 1939-40 will be relatively small.
The department is working steadily on the problem of finding the means of production for certain types of equipment for which there is no obvious source available. Energetic efforts are being put forth with respect to half a dozen specific requirements at the present time. It is not possible now to forecast whether we shall succeed in arranging for Canadian production, or whether we shall have to rely upon old country sources. Perhaps in one or two cases we shall develop Canadian sources, but in others, this may not be found economical. One cannot foretell with respect to which requirements the first solution may be found. Accordingly the department is asking for small votes for a variety of requirements under this heading in order that pressure may be kept up on all fronts until solutions have been found that utilize the authority granted by parliament for the expenditure of approximately S3,000,000 on new items.

The meaning of the objective may be better understood if it were stated that upon acquiring the items included in it the service could, from that point, proceed on a maintenance basis. This objective includes the proper weapons and stores of ammunition to put the militia service in a position to discharge with reasonable efficiency its share of the duty of national defence for Canada. With regard to engineer services and works, the amount allotted for construction of new buildings for the militia services for
1939-40 is slightly less than that approved for 1938-39. The estimates of 1939-40 provide for $2,367,165, whereas the vote for 1938-39 was $2,799,855, there being a decrease of $432,720. It is not anticipated that the repair and upkeep of buildings and works will require any greater sum during the current year. The items of new work to be undertaken are very widely distributed in comparatively small amounts. I shall give some of the larger items.
There will be a new building at Camp Borden for the accommodation of the Canadian armoured fighting vehicle school and the army service corps training centre, costing
