$100,000. At Kingston there will be further construction of the anti-aircraft training building and artillery park to the extent of $30,000. At Kingston Vimy barracks, there will be additional work on the parade ground, roads and grading, electrical system, water supply, sewer construction, et cetera, to an amount of $50,000.
There will be an expenditure of $45,000 on the Montreal St. Bruno rifle range. There will be new construction to the extent of $40,000 on the Bedford magazine at Halifax, and repairs and renewals to the extent of $26,500 at Fort McNab. There is $25,000 for continued development at Shilo camp, Manitoba. The completion of the building program at the joint service magazine at Esqui-malt will cost $73,000. The third stage of the construction of Pacific coast defences will total $900,000. The total cost of the entire program is estimated at $3,975,000, of which $1,995,000 has already been provided in the past two years, leaving a further requirement for next year of $1,080,000. At Dundurn camp, Saskatchewan, there will be further improvements to the extent of $22,000. Additional work will be done in all military districts, with reference to the following projects:
Niagara rifle range Winona, Ontario, rifle range Fort Frontenac barracks St. Johns, Quebec, barracks Valcartier camp Sussex camp
Kamloops joint service magazine Prince Albert and Victoria armouries Royal Military college
I come now to the program for the air services. For the air services there is being appropriated for the year 1939-40 the sum of $29,775,565, which is an increase of $18,089,048 over last year's vote. The appropriation for the Royal Canadian Air Force, permanent, is $20,085,238; for the Royal Canadian Air Force, non-permanent, the appropriation is $3,365,277; for civil government air operations, $325,050, and for training of pilots, $6,000,000. As already mentioned, the immediate objective of the department is to build up for the defence of Canada an air force consisting, on a peace time basis, of eleven permanent and twelve non-permanet squadrons, which is considered the minimum for any effective defence plan. The policy is to provide permanent force squadrons with a full complement of first line service aircraft in squadrons, with a reserve, and to provide non-permanent squadrons with one-third of their complement, consisting of elementary and advanced training aircraft, and a reserve. Further, it is intended to provide schools with the number of aircraft required to train new entries and replace wastage.
This objective involves the provision of 527 aircraft. Of this number approximately
59 per cent, or 312, represents the number of aircraft required to be available for active operations in squadrons. The remaining 215, including reserves, are required for training. To man a force of this size requires a permanent force of 525 officers and 4,500 airmen, a non-permanent force of 220 officers and 2,014 airmen, making a total of 745 officers and 6,514 airmen. Of the total number of officers, 599 would be pilots, the remaining 146 officers being employed on ground duties. A small proportion of airmen are also employed as pilots.
There has already been described the progress made towards attainment of this objective. Further progress is to be made out of current year's estimates as follows. Personnel: Aside from increases to be provided for in the vote for training of pilots, personnel of the Royal Canadian Air Force permanent force is to be increased by fourteen officers and 217 airmen, making a total of 231, making the establishment for the coming year 273 officers and 2,172 airmen, a total of 2,445 (including permanent officers and men attached to nonpermanent force for instruction, et cetera). Pay and allowances for this establishment will be $3,026,777-an increase of $159,873. For the permanent air force the principal other items in the appropriations are: for stores and equipment, $11,889,893; construction of buildings and works, $4,023,000. For the nonpermanent air force the principal items in the appropriations are: pay and allowances, $279,725; stores and equipment, $2,657,591; construction of buildings and works, $189,000, as well as the usual maintenance, transportation, medical and other charges.
New service type aircraft, in addition to training craft to be acquired out of the $6,000,000 training vote, will be ordered during the coming year as follows: for the permanent air force, eighty-eight; for the nonpermanent air force, nineteen, a total of one hundred and seven. In addition, there will be purchased forty-five spare engines. Planes to be purchased for the permanent air force will be as follows: six flying boats, six army cooperation planes, twelve general purpose twin engines, ten new type general recon-naisance twin engine planes, ten general purpose single engine, twenty-six fighters, eight-teen bombers twin engines.
For the non-permanent air force:	four
advanced trainer aircraft and fifteen observation aircraft. Of the above, fourteen fighters and the eighteen twin engine bombers will be purchased abroad for delivery within the fiscal year. The others will be manufactured in Canada and cannot be completed for delivery within the year, but deliveries of these will be made very quickly. Total payments during the coming fiscal year on the above
Supply-National Defence

new aircraft will be: for the permanent force, 84,471,003; for the non-permanent force, $1,173,646, a total of $5,644,649, leaving to be paid in 1940-41, when it is expected that delivery will be effected, a balance of $2,350,000.
Out of the appropriation for stores and equipment there will be payable on seventy-four aircraft, already ordered and not delivered, the following sums: on fifty-two aircraft for the permanent Royal Canadian Air Force, $2,292,169; on twenty-two aircraft for the non-permanent Royal Canadian Air Force, $820,030, a total of $3,112,199. The total cost of the planes ordered during the past two years on which this balance of payment remains to be made was: fifty-two for permanent Royal Canadian Air Force, $3,439,043; twenty-two for non-permanent Royal Canadian Air Force, $1,091,434, a total of $4,158,477.
It will be seen, having regard to what was explained with regard to progress during the past three years, that without the planes to be ordered from the 1939-40 estimates we have provided, in allowing for wastage, for 250 aircraft out of an objective of 527. The additional 107, to be ordered in the coming year will raise the total to 357, which is approximately two-thirds of the objective laid down for the twenty-three squadrons.
Progress payments made on planes under construction in the new aircraft industry in Canada, which these orders have assisted to develop, amount so far to approximately 45 per cent of the total. It is expected that all deliveries will be completed during the coming fiscal year.
It has taken longer to procure these aircraft from Canadian industry than would have been the case had they been bought abroad. This delay was considered well worth while, because the development in Canada of a future source of supply for service aircraft is in itself a major contribution to national defence. Until this department went into the market and sought to develop this domestic source of supply, the manufacture of modern service aircraft was an industry that did not exist in Canada. Whatever benefits may accrue to Canadian industry from the recent decision of the British air ministry to purchase aircraft in Canada are attributable to the policy of the Department of National Defence in fostering this Canadian industry, because the air ministry decided to deal only with firms which were already engaged in production. On the other hand, the decision of the British government to place orders in Canada will have several benefits to the Department of National Defence. On the strength of British orders additional plants and 
equipment will be brought into use; additional engineers and workers will be trained in the production of service craft and, due to the larger operations, the unit cost to the Canadian government of similar orders will be substantially reduced.
In addition to the new aircraft above enumerated, the department will purchase during 1939-40: thirty-eight new aircraft engines for the permanent air force; fifteen new aircraft engines for the non-permanent air force.
Construction of buildings and works. Out of the $4,023,000 to be expended on construction works for the Royal Canadian Air Force there will be further development of the program on both Atlantic and Pacific coasts, as well as the provision of increased facilities at Trenton and Ottawa and the construction of a central repair depot at a site not yet finally determined. The chief activities on the Pacific coast will be as follows: At Patricia bay: completion of the grading, hard-surfacing the runways, construction of two hangars, one each for land planes and sea planes, barrack block, et cetera; at Prince Rupert: clearing and excavating of site, construction of slipway, apron, wireless station and storage tanks; at Aliford bay : completion of the apron, slipway and wharf; provision of light and power, construction of wireless station, storage tanks, et cetera; at the Kamloops magazine: officers' and men's quarters; at Vancouver: construction of radio station, stores building, pier and breakwater, additions and improvements to quarters, et cetera.
On the Atlantic coast the following will be the chief undertakings: at Dartmouth: construction of four hangars, grading and hard-surfacing of runways, et cetera; at Yarmouth: completion of grading and hard-surfacing runways; at Sydney: filling, levelling and hard-surfacing the runways, and construction of a road t-o the site; at Truro: grading and hard-surfacing the runways, completion of magazines, construction of tank and water supply, construction of quarters for officers and men. Other works will include: at Trenton: a training workshop, hospital construction, boundary lights and further grading and dredging; at Ottawa: construction of an additional hangar, hard-surfacing two runways, construction of a garage and married officers' quarters. At locations not yet decided there will be constructed a central repair depot and four direction finding and one wireless telegraph stations.
I come now, Mr. Chairman, to the $6,000,000 vote for the training of pilots. This coincides with the discussion which took place last year with respect to cooperation with the British authorities for the joint training of pilots. It

Supply-National Defence
covers the cost of individual instruction, teaching the young applicant what he needs to know about actual flying up to the point where he is able to take his place in an established squadron. The program laid down under this appropriation is intended to cover the training of 126 pilots for the Royal Canadian Air Force and the Royal Air Force. It includes:	(1) pay and allowances for the
pilots themselves and for the instructional and ground staff necessary to their training; (2) cost of the varied types of equipment required, including aircraft and engines, together with spares; (3) cost of buildings and construction work necessary to the scheme. These expenditures, as with the other national defence estimates this year, are classified as follows: ordinary, $2,771,840; capital, $3,228,160. The relatively large capital amount is for the acquisition of new equipment and buildings necessary for the addition of this large new program. For new buildings and works there will be required $932,000; for new aircraft and engines there will be required $2,123,160; barrack equipment will require $116,500; and aircraft spares, $56,500.
Because not all deliveries can be completed within the fiscal year, the appropriation for aircraft and engines involves a commitment of S641,840 aaginst the future, while the building program involves a future commitment of $120,000. Training will be conducted in three stages: (a) elementary training, which will be carried out at civilian schools at various places; (b) intermediate training, to be carried out at Camp Borden; (c) advanced training, chiefly at Trenton.
Personnel. The instructional and maintenance staff required for the intermediate and advanced stages to be carried out at Camp Borden and Trenton will require approximately sixty-eight officers and 600 airmen. It will be necessary to increase the air force by those numbers during the coming year. Key positions in the training scheme will be filled as far as possible from the existing complement of the Royal Canadian Air Force. The remainder will be appointed or enlisted from civil sources or from the auxiliary' active air force. The scheme will require ninety-three training aircraft, of which seventy-one will be required for active and immediate reserve purposes. The other twenty-two will be in reserve stores. Pay and allowances for personnel in the first year's operation will run to slightly more than one million dollars. The maintenance cost of stores and equipment in the first year is estimated at $1,319,000. This includes the items for fuel, overhaul of aircraft and engines, spare equipment, clothing, miscellaneous stores, et cetera. The whole estimate is based on existing regulations and the actual experience in administering them.
I would refer hon. members to the statement made by the Prime Minister in this house on July 1, 1938. I quote:
We are quite prepared in connection with our own establishments, to help in affording facilities to British pilots if that will be ol service to them.
And again:
We ourselves are prepared to have our own establishments here and to_ give in those establishments facilities to British pilots to come and train here.
Discussions on the basis of these statements have been proceeding. While the final detailed technical arrangements have still to be completed, it is possible to say now that agreement has been reached on a scheme whereby pilots from the United Kingdom will come to Canada to be given the intermediate and advanced stages of training under the auspices of the Canadian Department of National Defence.
iMr. BROOKS: Will that be training under our pilots or under the British pilots?

subtopic: SINGLE UNEMPLOYED MEN IN OTTAWA-QUESTION AS TO ACTION BY FEDERAL GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
I shall come to that in a moment, if my hon. friend will allow me. One of' the main reasons for sending men to train to Canada is that Canadian topographical and climatic conditions give opportunities for specialized training.
The duration of the scheme will be three years. It is contemplated that the number of pilots coming from the United Kingdom for training will not exceed fifty in any one year. It is planned that, after twelve months' experience of the working of the scheme, the actual costs involved should be investigated by representatives of the Department of National Defence and the air ministry jointly and that, if needs be, the basis of payment should be revised after such investigation.
There are already in existence three methods of entry of Canadian candidates for Royal Air Force commission: (a) two locally accepted Canadians may be selected and trained each year in Canada for permanent commissions in the Royal Air Force; (b) fifteen locally accepted Canadians are trained each year in Canada for short service commissions in the Royal Air Force; (c) one hundred and twenty applicants for short service commissions in the Royal Air Force are interviewed, medically examined and selected in Canada. All the foregoing methods of entry will remain in force, and their existence will not be affected by the introduction of the scheme referred to above.
Supply-National Defence

In regard to the question asked by my hon. friend it is anticipated that there will be a limited number of high grade instructors attached to our own instruction staff under the jurisdiction of the department here for purposes of training. I have not the exact figures at the moment, but shall be glad to get them.
Two other innovations are embodied in the program covered by the vote for "training of pilots": (1) initiation of the "short service commission" as a feature of the Royal Canadian Air Force establishment; (2) utilization of approved civilian flying clubs for the elementary stages of training.
In regard to short service commissions, present regulations provide that candidates for commissions in the permanent Royal Canadian Air Force are required to be graduates of the Royal Military College or of a Canadian university. This high standard has been based on the assumption that the permanent air force officers must all be competent to assume the most exacting technical and administrative duties of what is, in a sense, a very large engineering organization.
Two problems have developed during the period of rapid expansion during the past three years: (1) The extreme physical strain of active flying necessitates a certain amount of turn-over among the junior officers; there is a tendency for the force to become grounded through lack of physical fitness; (2) If all officers hold permanent commissions there will not be enough administrative posts for those who attain seniority in the service. Accordingly it has been decided to introduce a short service commission scheme similar to that in the Royal Air Force. The scheme contemplates 50 per cent permanent and 50 per cent short service officers ultimately. The period of service on the active list for short service commissions will be four years-to be followed by six years on the Royal Canadian Air Force reserve. The ordinary conditions as to physical fitness, nationality, et cetera, will be required. The educational standard, however, will be lower. The required standard will be the equivalent of junior matriculation, plus three or more senior matriculation subjects.
Candidates will be considered under three categories: (1) Those without previous flying experience who are unmarried and between eighteen and twenty-five years of age, inclusive; (2) Qualified pilots of the Auxiliary Active Air Force and the Royal Canadian Air Force reserve; (3) Commercial pilots.
Qualified candidates of the latter two categories who are married may be carried supernumerary to the married establishment.
Provision is made for the award of a limited number of permanent commissions to those

accepted for short service commissions. It will also be possible for a limited number to remain on medium service commissions-that is, to remain for an additional five years on the active list-making nine years in all. Candidates without previous flying experience will receive their elementary flying and ground training at civilian schools-namely, with the approved flying clubs.
Pay of the short service officers will be the same as that for general list officers, excepting that provisional pilot officers will receive $3.50 a day, augmented by fifty cents in lieu of rations and quarters, during the time of training at civilian flying schools.
Assistance in reestablishment in civil life for these young men after their four years' service is part of the program. Upon transfer to the reserve each officer will receive a gratuity calculated on the basis of $500 for each year of service, excepting the first year. In addition, 5 per cent of the pay of the short service officer will be deducted as deferred pay and returned to him on transfer to the reserve or on being gazetted out of the service, or to the estate of an officer who dies while on service. At the end of the ordinary four year term the young officer would thus leave the service with $1,500 cash, plus 5 per cent of all pay earned.
The civilian flying clubs have played an important role in the development of aviation in Canada. It is proposed now to assign them a definite role in the training of pilots for the Royal Canadian Air Force. As a result of the decision to train 126 pilots a year for the Royal Canadian Air Force and the Royal Air Force, the elementary stage of training is to be done through the instrumentality of the flying clubs. Canadian applicants will be trained by flying club instructors in flying club planes. The department will provide two planes to each approved club and the club will provide one plane. The instructors must have the standard certificates laid down by the force, and it is proposed to bring them in at the outset for refresher courses of instruction at Camp Borden. This will ensure equality of standards in the instruction at all clubs throughout the country.
The contract between the department and the flying clubs will be in the form of separate contracts with each club to which is assigned one or more pilot officers for training. The form of the contract was worked out with the flying clubs association, and the rates of compensation and other terms are based on the existing experience of the clubs, checked against departmental information. The clubs are endeavouring to render this vital service to our aerial defence without profit to their organizations. The club undertakes to pro-

Supply-National Defence
vide one training aircraft of approved type; the department agrees to furnish two additional planes. The club is to provide two instructors and contracts to carry out the training according to the syllabus laid down by the department. The club is to be paid on the basis of so much per flying hour, but in addition the department is to pay $200 to the club for each officer whose training is completed satisfactorily to the department.
A scale of compensation for lectures and instruction on ground subjects is also provided, and it is estimated that the department will pay in cash to the flying club a total of $840 with respect to the training of each pilot. Each of the three periods of training: (a) Elementary-with the flying clubs; (b)	intermediate-at Camp Borden; (c)
advanced-at Trenton, will be of approximately sixteen weeks duration, with one week between each stage for travelling. This permits the three stages of training to be completed in one year.
That completes a description of the estimates now before us for consideration. I should like now to approach more general conclusions with regard to the philosophy of defence.
To approach the broad question of defence in a scientific manner it is necessary to ask: First, what national or other interests shall in the last resort be defended by force of arms; second, from what quarter are these interests exposed to attack?
The general and particular defensive requirements, tasks, organization, composition, strength and distribution of the armed and other forces must be worked out in detail in the light of the interests to be defended and what they have to be defended against. President Roosevelt, in a recent memorable speech, held that there are forces in the world to-day that threaten not only national existence, but all that makes existence worth while. He said that three institutions, indispensable to America, are being challenged, and that the first of these, religion, is the source of the other two, democracy and international good faith.
Mr. Walter Lippmann described these as the most important landmarks in the history of western thought. In the New York Herald-Tribune of January 7, 1939, he said :
It marks the reconciliation which is now in progress, after more than >a _ century of destructive conflict, between patriotism, freedom, democracy and religion.
Again to quote Mr. Lippmann:
And so this message expresses a philosophy, as new to the president as it is new to the world that heard it, a philosophy which formulates in outline the positive answer of the west to the forces which threaten to destroy
the western world. One would greatly underestimate its significance in thinking of it only as a response to the challenge of nazism. It is in a much more important sense a response to those forces of moral disintegration which communism, fascism and nazism inherit and exploit .	.	. This message contains within
it. hy implication and in embryo, the _ outline of that reconstruction in their moral philosophy which the democracies must undertake if they are to survive.
These sentiments reflect Canadian opinion fully as much as that of the United States republic. In the light of this declaration it may be said that Canada should be prepared to defend by force of arms if necessary: (1) Our religion, our freedom and our institutions; (2) our coasts and coastal regions, our centres of population and industry, our main ports and the focal sea areas where trade routes converge in the vicinity of our main ports; (3) our neutrality in a war in which Canada is not a belligerent; (4) internal order.
As to the extent to which the armed forces of other powers influence the form and scale of attack to which the above interests may be subject, large scale attacks by enemy forces upon our coasts and our trade at its congested points adjacent to our main ports and focal sea areas are out of the question at the present time, for the following reasons:	.
1.	Geography, distance of bases.
2.	World political situation.
3.	Existence of British and United States navies.
On the north Atlantic the British fleet, whose task it is to keep open vital sea lines of communication, is predominant and is sufficiently strong either to destroy or to contain any potential hostile navy. So long as that condition exists, assuming that Canada for any reason become involved in conflict, a major expedition against our east coast is considered to be practically impossible.
On the United States side of the north Pacific the United States fleet is equally predominant, and any hostile fleet contemplating an attack has to bear this risk in mind, also the risks inherent in the existence of the Singapore base.
It is to be assumed that hostile fleets will be restrained and constrained by the presence of the British and American fleets on the Atlantic and the Pacific, but under modern conditions complete blockade is impossible, and attack upon Canada's overseas trade at its congested points will be by way of minor raiding forces. Raids are a possibility, in fact a probability, but their strength in the contingencies mentioned would be limited by the strength and position of the British and United States or other allied navies.
Supply-National Defence

Beyond our focal sea areas Canadian, overseas trade receives a measure of protection by the British navy on the north Atlantic route and by the United States navy on the coastal route to the Panama canal. Therefore Canada's responsibility with respect to protection of her trade is limited to the protection of our own ports and of the relatively short distances between those ports and the main trade routes policed by the great navies of Britain and the United States.
In regard to internal order and neutrality, the hazards to be encountered would be less than those coming from enemy action, therefore the forces required to resist external attack would be adequate for these purposes, should any such need arise.
In regard to coasts, coastal regions, ports, focal sea areas, inland centres of population and industry, a minor combined sea, land and air force expedition launched against our coast for the purpose of destroying something of strategic or commercial value, or for the purpose of securing an advanced base from which hostile sea and/or air force raiders could operate against our focal sea areas, our main ports and centres of population and industry inland, might be directed against our own interests or against those of a friendly power, and so has application to all aspects of our direct defence, including the protection of our neutrality. Sporadic hit and run raids by one ship of the line or by one or more cruisers or submarines or armed merchantmen, each carrying one or more aircraft, might have the purpose of destroying vulnerable points by small landing parties, or of raiding focal sea areas and main ports by sea and/or air, of raiding inland centres of population and industry by air.
The forms and scales of attack to which our religion, freedom and institutions are exposed is difficult to estimate, and can perhaps be best expressed in the words of Right Hon. Anthony Eden on January 14, 1939, when he discussed the realities of the situation that confronts the world. He said:
In the autocratic states there is a vitality and an enthusiasm on behalf of the faith that has been fostered among them, which it would be a grave mistake to belittle. We may dislike the methods, the suppression of criticism, the ruthless use of propaganda, and deplore the loss of individual freedom of thought and action, yet the results are there in mass enthusiasm and national fervour, and they are very formidable indeed.	*
From the earliest years a child, if living under a ^ dictatorship, is trained to dedicate his or her life to an ideal of nationhood constantly placarded and paraded. No opportunity is left for doubts or questions. The propaganda machine and all the resources of a highly organized state are there to see to that. He or she is a cog in a machine, and in most cases is well content to be so.

I come now to the defence measures required to protect Canada's interests against the probable risks. In the first place, there is the preservation of internal order; this is a task for land forces and consists mainly of protecting vulnerable points against sabotage. The recently adopted principle that vulnerable points to be guarded by the militia must be of national importance, and that transportation companies, power companies, et cetera must be prepared to take certain protective measures at their own expense, has met with considerable success. This policy reduces the number of troops required. Their duties are, internal order, guarding of internment camps, and cooperation with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in rounding up enemy aliens.
In regard to neutrality, if indeed that is possible now, it requires the constant patrol of the coastal area by auxiliary surface craft and aircraft in order to spot the location of any temporary refueling base for submarines or aircraft from which such craft could operate against United States shipping and other targets within aerial reach; bombing aircraft to destroy such bases when found, and the retention of means to despatch a small expedition of all arms to destroy the base, should bombing aircraft not be equal to the task.
With regard to focal sea areas, coasts, main ports, inland centres of population and industry, the defence of these areas and points requires, for focal sea areas, sea and air forces capable of finding and destroying hostile surface craft, submarine or aircraft raiders. This task would require reconnaissance, fighter, bomber and torpedo carrying aircraft, and adequate naval strength. In regard to coasts, main ports, inland centres of population and industry, it would require fixed coast and anti-aircraft defences at and in the vicinity of the main ports, improvised coast and anti-aircraft defences at strategical points, anti-aircraft defences at important inland centres of population and industry, ground troops to protect and man the coast and anti-aircraft defences, to watch important points on the coast, and to provide a small reserve for the unexpected; naval craft for examination services, mine laying, mine sweeping and cooperation on seaward defence; army cooperation aircraft to work with the fixed coast defences, and fighter aircraft to work in conjunction with the anti-aircraft defences.
In regard to the larger issues, as I mentioned before, no one can foretell the extent to which the resources of Canada might come to be committed in a world-wide struggle between ruthless aggressive forces of conquest and destruction, against which the combined

Supply-National Defence
democratic and liberty loving peoples would be compelled to unite for the defence of their freedom and their ideals. Each democratic country, once involved, would have to contribute her best efforts according to her capacity, resources and geographical position. The extent of the effort required would be governed by the scope, intensity and length of the struggle.
Then, very briefly, the real tasks of our three services may be outlined. The land forces may be expected to be required:
1.	To man all coast and anti-aircraft defences.
2.	To maintain a reserve for protective garrisons for coast defence and other strategic points.
3.	To provide guards for vulnerable points of national importance.
4.	To provide such assistance as may be required by the civil authorities in the rounding up of enemy aliens.
5.	To provide guards for internment camps.
6.	To have a reserve force available to meet the unexpected.
7.	Should the eventualities of intensive conflict necessitate it, for the fundamental protection of Canadian institutions and Canadian ideals.
The militia system of Canada to-day is capable of having ready, subject to public demand and parliamentary approval, a substantial force ready for active service within six months after mobilization. Our militia system of a large non-permanent force, with a small permanent establishment to provide highly trained staff and instruction, is precisely calculated for the necessities which have just been described. It is this desirability of capacity for quick expansion which explains the high proportion of officers and non-commissioned officers on peace establishments.
The coast defence units are localized in the fortress areas concerned. The reserve units are localized throughout Canada, and have been allotted in accordance with population ratios.
In regard to coastal and anti-aircraft defence, troops allotted to these categories comprise artillery, engineers, signals, infantry, ordnance, army service corps, and medical units. The total peace establishment of such units is about 20,000, actual strength being 12,000 and training strength 9,000.
Troops allotted to reserve consist of skeleton units, comprising those required to form one cavalry division, and six divisions of ancillary troops. No such divisions exist at present, but Canada does maintain sufficient skeleton
units to form that number of formations on mobilization, and a scheme for such divisions is always in readiness for use. For these purposes the establishment is: peace establishment, about 65,000; actual strength, 37,000; training strength, 31,000.
Concerning equipment, most of the efforts of the department in the past three years have been directed to the objective of providing the equipment necessary to the discharge of the duties which have just been described, according to the organization plan just set forth.
Concerning the air force, I have already mentioned the objective, to build up eleven permanent squadrons and twelve non-permanent squadrons. The tasks of the air force are:
1.	Air action in defence of points of national importance from air attack in conjunction with ground anti-aircraft defences and observer corps.
2.	In cooperation with the sea forces to reconnoitre coastal regions, focal sea areas and vicinities.
3.	Operating alone or in cooperation with the sea and/or land forces to destroy hostile surface craft or aircraft or land force raiders.
4.	Air observation for coast defence artillery.
With regard to these tasks the air force has
a tremendous advantage over the other two services. The inevitable growth of civil aviation in a natural flying country such as Canada has provided and will continue in greater degree to provide a reserve of experienced pilots. The accompanying growth of the aircraft industry and its recent expansion into the production of service type aircraft will complete the twin essential bases of an effective military air force, namely, a reserve of experienced pilots, and the means of producing major types of equipment and armament within our own borders.
The existing twenty-three squadrons of the Royal Canadian Air Force are grouped into three commands, western, eastern and central. The western command consists of eight squadrons and one flight. The eastern command consists of nine squadrons. All of these seventeen squadrons are allotted to duties of direct defence. The remaining six squadrons are in the central command and would be available for use as a reserve in accordance with exigencies that might arise.
Sea forces. Naval defence policy, in cooperation with the land and air forces, aims at the security of both coasts and the focal sea areas in the vicinity of the main ports against the probable forms and scales of seaborne attack. The tasks of the navy are:
Supply-National Defence

1.	In cooperation with the air force to reconnoitre coastal maritime regions, focal sea areas and their vicinities.
2.	In cooperation with the land and air forces to destroy surface craft and submarine raiders.
3.	To provide examination services at our main seaports.
4.	In cooperation with the land forces to
provide anti-motor torpedo boat and antisubmarine protection for our main seaports.
5.	To keep the approaches to our main seaports clear of mines.
I think I can safely say that I have now covered, in the first place the situation that confronted the Department of National Defence in 1935, and in the second place the steps taken between 1935 and the present time to remedy the deficiencies and close the gaps found to exist at that time.
I now approach the conclusion of my remarks on this occasion. I have endeavoured to give an accurate description of the actual situation that existed when I was entrusted with the responsibility of the direction of the Department of National Defence. I have endeavoured to inform the house and the country, perhaps in elaborate and laborious detail, in regard to the progress made during the last three years. It has been stated here and elsewhere that we have nothing to show for the moneys that have been voted by parliament. That, I suggest, in view of what I have placed upon record this afternoon, is a thoughtless, unfair and somewhat harmful statement. I trust that the information I have given to-day will prevent a repetition of such unworthy allegations and ill-informed statements.
I have also endeavoured to inform the committee as thoroughly as possible in regard to the purposes for which the estimates now being presented are required. I know, Mr. Chairman, they may be attacked from two angles. There may be those who conscientiously believe and will say that we are spending too much on national defence, seeing that a measure of economic distress exists in our country. My answer to them would be, with great respect:	Can you have social or economic security if national security is imperilled in our country? There also may be those who, with equal honesty, will say that the estimates are not large enough. That may be indeed a fair criticism, but when we cast our minds back three years I think that we will all admit that we have progressed far along the road of realization of responsibility. We may have to go further, much further, but that is a question for the future.

These estimates are for the purpose of our national security in Canada. We in this house are all deeply proud of our kinship in the family of British nations. We are all deeply conscious of our responsibilities and obligations in that free and friendly partnership. We are deeply grateful, I believe, for the continuing manifestation of earnest and sincere friendship shown to us by the grandest neighbour any nation ever had, the republic to our south and beside us. We rejoice that a great newspaper such as the New York Times could say, as it did, in its editorial columns of February 21, 1939:
It is a sign of the times and of the changed values in the contemporary world that this greatest of British armament programs should cause no concern to our side of the Atlantic. We do not regard it with suspicion. We do not *ask for "parity" as we once did in this or that category of naval strength. We do not fear an increase of British power-we welcome it, for we know that while there can be no question of an alliance between the British and ourselves, the facts of geography and the lessons of history have created -a common interest between Britain and the United States. That common interest is an orderly and stable world.
I have also endeavoured to analyse the cardinal principles and fundamental features of Canadian defence policy. Two years ago I stated in this house that Canada was becoming defence conscious. To-day, in the light of the developments that have taken place, the menace of the hour, and the clouds on the horizon, I think it is safe to say that Canada is becoming defence anxious. No country ever had a greater heritage, a more vivid consciousness of freedom. No country ever had a deeper sense of national pride, and no country has ever possessed a more decent and dauntless people. That consciousness of freedom, that national pride, that fine, free fibre of our people, must be mobilized through our realization of our great responsibilities and through the knowledge that science and invention have made isolation a myth and a dream. They must be mobilized along the avenue of real and earnest cooperation, cooperation within the commonwealth of our own family of nations and cooperation for the preservation of the principles of liberty and freedom with the kin democracies of the world.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, may I venture to suggest that it is our earnest hope and prayer that out of the shifting issues and changing policies of these times, out of the dangers that seem to confront the liberty-loving democracies of the world, there will emerge three great principles, ultimately

Supply-National Defence
coalescing into one: the security of our own people, the solidarity of the empire and the preservation of freedom itself in our time.

subtopic: SINGLE UNEMPLOYED MEN IN OTTAWA-QUESTION AS TO ACTION BY FEDERAL GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first I should like to express my pleasure that the minister has been able to return to the house this afternoon to deliver this statement. I know that for some time he has desired to make a statement for the information of hon. members, and it must have been extremely annoying two days ago when indisposition prevented him from accomplishing his desire. So I congratulate him upon having been able to do so to-day.
It would seem almost like cruelty to animals to continue this debate before an exhausted house which for two hours and fifteen minutes has listened to one of the most comprehensive exhortations, shall I say, to have been delivered in this house for some time. The first part of the minister's remarks was devoted to the past, the present and the future, and during the course of that portion of his address he quoted at some length from recent utterances by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), also referring to the fact that my hon. leader (Mr. Manion) had expressed his opinions on the questions with which he was dealing. Perhaps it might not be out of place for me to refer to what my leader did say, in order that it might be placed in juxtaposition to the other remarks quoted by the minister. I should like to point out that on March 27 of this year, three days before the Prime Minister's speech in the house and four days before the speech of the Minister of Justice, my hon. leader made a public statement in which he made his position perfectly clear. That position was stated as follows:
1.	That there should be no profiteering in war-time.
2.	He quoted his predecessor, Mr. Bennett, to the effect that when Britain is at war Canada is automatically at war, because the enemy would consider us liable to attack; and the leader of the opposition supported that position.
3.	He stated that neutrality by Canada in a war in which Britain was participating was impossible, and he supported full cooperation in every way by Canada with Britain in wartime, short of conscription of men to serve outside Canada.
4.	He stood out for adequate home defence for Canada.
5.	He believed that we should have an understanding with the United States, and
that there should be a united front of all democracies against world domination by any dictator.
In my opinion that fills out the picture drawn by the minister in his reference to the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice.
It is not my purpose, Mr. Chairman, to attempt, even were that possible, to follow in any detail the statement made by the minister. His object, I know, was to give every available bit of information to members of this committee in order to facilitate discussion when we get into the estimates and to enable that discussion to be carried on in an informative manner. It would appear to me that in the very short statement I propose to make this afternoon the note I should strike is that the position in which Canada finds herself to-day is entirely different from that in which Canada has found herself at any other period of her history. From confederation to the time of the great war Canada had her militia. Air defence was unheard of. Two or three attempts had been made to provide at least the foundation of a naval defence force. For this reason and for that the force did not come into being. Frankly, Canada relied for the defence of her coasts, her commerce and her neutrality upon the Royal Navy; and the Royal Navy has of course always been kept up by the taxpayers of the United Kingdom. To that upkeep Canada made no contribution.
It would be impossible to compare Canada's condition to-day with the period of the war. It would be just as impossible to compare it with the period which existed immediately after the war, when demobilization was the main business of the day, and when retrenchment was evidently necessary. And that condition carried on until the end of 1934.
Canada, in her position as a member of the League of Nations, in concert with her fellow members of the league, was just as imbued as any other nation of the whole world with the pursuit of peace. It was Canada's desire that it might be proved that the war which had just been completed was to end war. True it was that there were some who doubted it. True it is that their numbers increased as that period drew towards an end.
Then, in the year 1934, it became more and more evident to Canada and the rest of the peace-seeking world that one of the great nations of the world was intending to strike out her signature to documents, to go back on her spoken word, and to throw off the shackles of the Versailles treaty, and an entirely new state of affairs was placed before the world.
Supply-National Defence

But there is one reason to my mind greater than all others to demonstrate the fact that Canada's condition to-day, the condition of defence which she faces, is different from that which faced her at any other period of her existence. I refer to the fact that this parliament passed the statute of Westminster. The foundation of that statute was the resolution in the 1926 imperial conference, to which Canada deliberately and delightedly consented. And when we passed the statute of Westminster we said to the world that we stood on our own feet. Canada then said that she gloried in her position. And whilst there were shoutings to that effect, there were, too, whisperings of the fact that Canada, having adopted that glorious and honourable position, must henceforth seek to defend herself more potently than she had defended herself in the past.
We trusted, as did the other nations of the league, in the integrity of the other nations who joined in the cause of disarmament. True, we can be wise after the event, and say that we went too far. There are hundreds- there are millions to-day who consider that Great Britain, leading the pace in disarmament, went too far. But is it fair to be wise after the event? Will not the students of history, going back over that period, give some praise to Great Britain and those who followed her in the attempt she made to live up to .the spoken word and to the signed document which enabled the world to move towards disarmament?
It appears to me the same remark could be made with regard to the minister's reference to the condition in which he found his department when he took over as minister. It reminded me, Mr. Chairman, of the byelection in Victoria, when the minister announcing that he did not wish to make any use of expenditures for defence purposes at the time of an election, felt constrained to do so-and did so. On this occasion the minister draws attention to the fact that he would not be critical, and that he was merely stating facts. And yet it leaves a taste in my mouth that is extremely akin to partisanship. However, it is a factual truth that the minister found those three branches of the defence of Canada in a poorer condition than a)t the end of 1935 they should have been, and he quite properly proceeded to improve it.
But through those years, when disarmament ruled, was the government of that day to be blamed because it voted only sufficient barely to keep up the three branches of the service? We are a democratic people. Whatever its colour may be, the government of the day, if it be a wise government, is dependent

for its policies on its reading of the opinion held by the public. I ask you, Mr. Chairman: Would it have been possible through those years of disarmament for a government to come before the House of Commons and ask parliament to vote increased sums for national defence purposes? It has been possible since to do so, and this government has done it. It was its obvious duty to do it But have not all the salient facts on which such matters are based been entirely changed since those days?
We barely maintained the Canadian navy. When an auxiliary vessel was wrecked, we did not replace her. We barely maintained the militia services. When equipment and munitions were depleted, they were barely replaced. Retrenchment took place in the air force, and planes became obsolete. But the atmosphere of those days was entirely different from the atmosphere of to-day. And the minister would have been recreant in his duty if on assuming office he had not made himself cognizant of all these facts, and then laid before his council his expression of opinion with regard to rectifying them. Many, many times have the figures showing the per capita expenditures of the nations which go to make up the British commonwealth of nations been laid before the House of Commons. Canada has not shown up well in the comparison. I am interested to note that again this afternoon the minister has tabled figures which will more nearly bring the comparison up to date. So with the statement the minister has made assisting us in the discussion which will take place, it will be possible, I believe, to arrive at least at our own opinions in regard to the wisdom of the suggestions and the expenditures of money to be made.
What have we now? We have a small but highly efficient Canadian navy. We know it is efficient because we are able to measure it against the yardstick of the Royal Navy. Last month our six destroyers and our auxiliary vessels carried out combined exercises with the squadron in the Atlantic, and I am given to understand that our ships carried out their portions of the exercises with distinction. It is true that they ought to be good. All our young officers are trained in the Royal Navy for four years, dating from entry as a cadet to the end of the examinations which produce an acting sub-lieutenant. Those four years are spent in ships and establishments of the Royal Navy. True, their pay and allowances are found by this country. But, this country makes no contribution to the highly valued service which we receive from the Royal Navy in connection with the training of our young officers.

Supply-National Defence
Unfortunately there is perhaps nothing that
is more liable to deterioration than a warship. While we have to-day six efficient torpedo boat destroyers, besides auxilary vessels, we should remember that two of these torpedo boat destroyers were built ten years ago. These boats were purchased to replace two other destroyers which could hardly be kept in commission. Three years ago we purchased two more destroyers from the Royal Navy to replace two destroyers which required such major refitting that it was not considered advisable to spend the money. That made four destroyers; last year the government purchased two more so that we now have six. Efficient though they are to-day, let us not forget that they are of a class which has been set aside by the Royal Navy as being obsolescent, but not obsolete. Within a very few years we shall find ourselves faced with the necessity of purchasing new destroyers to replace the present equipment.
Our militia is divided into the permanent force and the non-permanent active militia. I think it is quite realized that the permanent force is a small but extremely efficient force, whose duties are largely instructional. It is a matter of great regret to me that the estimates for the permanent force have not been increased. The engineering and ordnance services are undermanned and overworked, and the expenditures we have been making on munitions and fortifications have added to the work of these units. The number of trained instructors available to do the work of training in connection with the non-permanent active militia is such that applications from the non-permanent active militia have to be turned down.. I regret that it has been found impossible to increase the vote for the nonpermanent active militia as well as for the permanent forces. A few months ago a balance sheet of one of the units of the non-permanent active militia was laid before me, and I was shocked at the amount of money which it is necessary for the officers, non-commissioned officers and men of the non-permanent active militia to put up in order to keep up the efficiency of their unit. I am delighted to hear that the minister is proposing expenditures on these units, and I believe he referred to boots. These are articles which have been urgently needed.
It must be remembered that when after long consideration the reorganization of the nonpermanent active militia was eventually carried out, it meant that we set up units which required modem equipment. I think the minister will have to tell us when we deal with the item that many of the nonpermanent active militia units are without
necessary mechanized equipment, instruments, guns and so on which are required in order to train, and much more so in order to use efficiently. The recompense received by a unit of the non-permanent active militia is based upon the numbers of days spent in camp. It seems to me that so long as we look upon the non-permanent active militia as the back-bone of our defence, especially now that we recognize the different position in which Canada is placed, it will be necessary to increase drastically the amounts allowed to these militia units. It will be necessary to increase the training time in order to give more recognition to these men who volunteer for training after they have spent time at their ordinary work. Perhaps it would be better if I curtailed my remarks on this matter until we have had an opportunity to digest the enormous quantity of information the minister has laid before us. Before I sit down, let me say that towards the end of his remarks the minister touched upon one most necessary consideration. I think there are three things which the public will want to ascertain from this discussion. The first is: What have we received for the $90,000,000 spent in the last three years? It is true the minister explained this during his speech, but he read it with such rapidity that it was impossible to assimilate it.
Second, the public will want to know whether the progress which has been attained since the minister took charge of this department is as great as it should have been. We must remember that he himself has admitted, and everybody connected with the department knows that in future it is perfectly hopeless to rely for our needs upon Great Britain. The minister himself has told us how he set up an inquiry into industry in this country. I am sorry to say that when this inquiry was first instituted it was credibly reported to me that the political tinge of the company was looked into before it was examined. 1 believe that this was drawn to the attention of the minister and I understand that it has been changed entirely. I have no doubt that today there are few firms in Canada capable of making anything that could be used for defence, the names of which are not on the list and upon which a report has not been made as to their capacity to produce.

I have a short second question. How does it come about that under existing relief legislation of this kind, farmers and fishermen are treated in one way, and industrial workers, the other 50 per cent of the people, in another way? How does it come about that there is not an equality of treatment in respect of these protective measures, bonuses, subventions and subsidies? I cannot understand it. Why not under part II, in the alternative, give chartered banks the power and invest them with concurrent jurisdiction to make these small personal loans, because they are personal loans? That is what a bank is for; it is to advance money on the security of a man's salary and wages and his job. The lack of credit for white-collar workers compared with the favoured class, the farmers-although they do not get much, either-and the fishermen, was referred to in the price spreads investigation. I proposed in 1935, under a similar bill, that we should empower the banks, even if it were only by enabling legislation, to make these personal loans.
I wish the minister would consider a moment the cases I cited last night. I will not detain the committee more than a couple of minutes, but I wish to remind them what happens when an industrial worker who is out of work is in need of money. He has probably bought a house with a first mortgage, has obtained a second mortgage, and also has a chattel mortgage, 'bill of sale, and lien on his property. He goes to the bank, and under the scheme of the Minister of Finance he has a hard time to get a loan to improve his property, while he can get no personal loan from anybody. He has medical, hospital, insurance and other bills to meet, yet he has to pay two per cent a month, or twenty-four per cent a year, to discharge a few doctors' bills. I know a number of physicians, and they hate to take his money. I have sat in my day on five or six hospital boards, and I know well that physicians are ashamed to take the money when they find that it comes from one of these shark loan companies.
The government of the day are, I think, very unfair about these particular matters, the different rates to which I have referred. If there is to 'be class legislation in this country for one section, legislation like this bill, parts I and H, the people should know what is the purpose of the government. I suggest that the minister should amend the section

Small Loans
to give enabling legislation. There are many cities and towns which have no loan company of this kind. Persons in small cities who wish to borrow have to come down to Toronto in a boat or train and in a bus to the centre of the city to seek these loans. From my office I see every day a bus stop in front of our building where there is located one of the old pioneer companies which started this kind of racket; for that is what it is, and it was referred to in the British House of Commons as a racket. If the minister wants to have up-to-date legislation, let him make the bill workable. He will never gain anything by a policy like this. This particular kind of legislation, dealing with personal loans, is only in its infancy. Where did personal loans come from previously? They came from members of parliament, aldermen, people like that, who would lend a fellow ten or twenty-five dollars or endorse his note at the bank. He would probably pay, although sometimes he did not.
The present bill is going to be a flat failure from the start. It will not be workable. While the minister provides under another clause for inspection by the inspector of insurance, such action will amount to little or nothing. How can one inspector in Ottawa here deal with nine provinces, or even with the city I come from, and Hamilton, Oakville, and Halifax? When under the authority of this measure someone wants to lend a man three hundred dollars, how can the inspectors check him up, when the payment is a dollar a week or a dollar a month, to find out whether the legislation is being complied with?
The present government started off these companies in 1927 and 1928. There was a great deal of opposition to it on this side of the house. We did not believe in that legislation. It took the companies out of the Interest Act, the Money Lenders Act and the Companies Act, and made them a law to themselves, unregulated by any law, human or divine, and look where it has landed this country. It has put, in my constituency alone, dozens of industrial workers on relief. I know that to be a fact. This bill may be drafted by lawyers and experts and gentlemen in the minister's office and other places; but let me tell him this, as far as offering any relief to the industrial workers is concerned, it will be a flat failure from the start. I hope that this legislation will not be passed. I hope that when it goes to another part of this building it will be thrown out, because that is what should be done with it; it should be thrown out of the high court of parliament.

Mr. Varcoe's opinion is as follows:
Dear Sir,
You ask to be advised what the effect would be of omitting from the proposed small loans interest act the provision for the repeal of the Money Lenders Act. Section 6 of that aot provides that no money lender shall charge a rate of interest greater than twelve per centum per annum. The question is whether this section 6 would be superseded or stand repealed as being repugnant to the provisions of the proposed statute.
The view that commends itself to me is that section 6 aforesaid relates to the nominal rate of interest, i.e., the compensation payable to the lender which the parties choose to call interest; the lender may not charge under the name of interest more than the statutory rate. On the other hand, the proposed small loans interest act-should it become law-will limit the total charges, whether called interest by the parties or otherwise, to two per centum per month. It appears to me that these two enactments may consistently be said to stand side by side.
Then you require to be advised whether the enactment of the small loans interest >aet will preclude the provinces from dealing with service charges. It is not my opinion that by enacting this legislation parliament will have occupied the legislative field so as to preclude any action by the provincial legislation. On the contrary, I would think that the provinces could deal with service charges in just the same manner and to the same effect as at present, subject only to the qualification that the total cost of a loan must not exceed two per centum per month.
Yours truly,
F. P. Varcoe.

speechtext:
All I can do is to read the evidence of Mr. Dobson, president of the Canadian Bankers Association, which appears at page 126 of the proceedings of the banking and commerce committee of last year:
Now, if your committee should recommend and the government should decide to ask us to cooperate in the small loans field and provide an increased rate for monthly payment loans, I believe it is quite possible and probable that some other banks might then decide to take up that extended loan field. I do not mean to say they are going to take the business away from the small loan companies and go right through with that type of business. I do not believe for a moment that the small loan companies are not going to stay in business. I believe they are required there, but the banks might extend their field further, that is all.
The banking and commerce committee recommended against an extension of banking facilities along this line. Perhaps I should refer the hon. gentleman to the reasons then given. I do not know that I altogether subscribe to these reasons, but at least they are deserving of consideration; I have not formed an opinion on them. The chairman of the banking and commerce committee is here and probably could amplify the reasons which the bankers gave. I quote from the committee's report:
Your committee discussed at length a proposal that parliament should encourage the chartered banks to expand their personal loan services; but it was the consensus of opinion that such action should not be taken without carefully considering the effect on general bank-71492-206
ing policy. The Canadian banking system is generally regarded as organized to finance industrial productive effort and facilitate the movements of trade and commerce; and, as illustrated by the restriction of loans on real estate, banking regulations are expressly designed to maintain the liquidity of banking assets.
Before encouraging Canadian banks to engage upon a greater volume of consumers' credit, it would appear to be the part of wisdom to have further information as to the relation between consumers' credit and business depressions. Quite obviously unemployment creates difficulty in the discharge of debt obligations; and it is then when threatened with financial crisis- that Canada depends upon its banking system to preserve its social solvency.
As custodians of the people's savings, it may well be that the chartered banks should not be called upon to arrange their investments so that, in the unfortunate event of crisis, we should find public savings converted into small loans on personal security which, under normal conditions, are regarded as tolerably safe only when administered by highly specialized organization.
Apart from these reasons, which are carefully thought out, I may say that it occurred to me-I am really quite an amateur in this business-'that if the banks went into the small loan business and were charging about 12 per cent, inclusive of all charges, on small loans; I believe the law limits them to 7 per cent for interest proper-the tendency would be for a number of applicants for loans in the regular course of business to be referred to the small loans department. That would be a real danger, it seems to me, if the banks were carrying on this business along with their ordinary commercial business. In the province from which I come nearly everyone who borrows money borrows it from the banks in the usual course of business, but a good many of them do not expect to pay it back on the maturity of the note. I am afraid that if the banks had a small loans department a good many loan applicants would be referred to that department, which means that the banks would be charging them a very much higher rate of interest. But that is only my personal opinion.

whose loans run into hundreds of millions of dollars, if not billions. So I do not think that factor influenced the banks in their decision. Mr. Chairman, I should like to express some views on this bill. Before doing so, may I pay a tribute to the minister and to those who have supported the bill. I believe they have been sincere, I believe that they have been imbued with the idea that this bill will tend to hold stationary the needs of those poor people who are in distress to the extent that they have to borrow money to carry on. Having stated this, I want to submit one or two considerations to the committee. I share largely the view of the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens), with whom I am not always in agreement, that the passage of this bill would indicate to the people of Canada that the parliament of Canada was authorizing and encouraging needy men of small means to borrow money at rates of 24 and 26 per cent per annum.
To-day the banks pay 1J per cent on funds that are deposited. Under the successful guidance of our finance minister, Canada has been able to reduce the rates of interest paid upon our national debt from 5 and 51 per cent to 3 and 3J per cent. If we are to believe the economists in every group in the house, this country of great natural resources is carrying a burden, by way of interest charges on our national debt, which increases unemployment and stifles our national progress. Yet our debt is being carried at rates of 3, 3i and 4 per cent per annum, and we are told the country is strangled because of the rates of interest which we have to pay. It is suggested that the rates of 24 and 26 per cent mentioned in this bill are necessary because these usurious companies cannot afford to lend the money at a lower rate. My view is that if that is true, and I think we ought to accept the evidence upon which that statement is based, then the sooner this parliament says to these needy borrowers, "We will shut you off and prevent you from putting * yoke of that kind round your neck," the greater service we will render to men who are in need. How can a man making $145 a month pay such interest rates?
I know something of the practices of these companies from my experience in the courts, and I know something of the conditions under which they would hope to operate because of my knowledge of my own constituency of Parry Sound. In more than one small community in that constituency most of the workers are engaged in seasonal employment, the men working from the opening of navigation in the spring until the close in the fall. The

majority of the men in these communities are receiving no wage cheques during the winter months and they rely upon the credit advanced by the local grocer, the local doctor and the other merchants in order to get through the non-productive months of the year. When the spring comes round and they are again receiving their cheques, they pay off honestly and fairly out of their wages during the season the debts they contracted during the winter. I want none of these loan companies to invade communities in my district and lend money at 24 or 26 per cent. The result would be that instead of the local merchants or doctors receiving one hundred dollars of a workman's earnings, the loan sharks would go away with twenty-four or twenty-six dollars and leave the man with seventy-six or seventy-four dollars to distribute among his local creditors. Is that the assistance which the parliament of Canada wants to hold out?

subtopic: LIMITATIONS OF POWERS OF MONEY-LENDERS WITH RESPECT TO COST TO BORROWER, ETC.

My friend says it is robbery. Do not let us be extravagant in our condemnation in this matter. Let us view it from a fair point of view, and let us appreciate whether, when we put opportunities before needy people to borrow money at extravagantly usurious rates, we are befriending them, or rather are encouraging them to their own downfall. That is the way in which I view this legislation.
Let me conclude by saying that it has been pointed out by many students of economics- by the minister, for whom I have the greatest respect-that this is supposed to be the best we can do under the circumstances. Well, is the best we can do brought about because we have permitted usury to gain a stranglehold. in Canada; or is it because the British North America Act stands in our way, as in part it does, in solving this problem as regards provincial and federal legislation? Let me again join in the hope expressed by the hon. member for Kootenay East when he suggested that the Canadian Bank of Commerce might be joined in this matter by other chartered banks when they realize the injustices of the present practice; or perhaps a corporation, although not backed by all the banks, might be formed to supply the needs of needy men at decent and bearable rates of interest. If that should be accomplished through a candid discussion of this bill we shall have achieved something.
I say to the minister that if this bill carries, with the power of inspection which he is assuming as against both licensed and unlicensed money lenders, he should speed up

and equip that department with the fullest of plenary powers, so that during the next twelve months, before we convene again, he will be able to analyse what I regard as a nefarious racketeering business and come back to this house with instances, causes and effects, which will enable us, when a year from now we discuss this problem, to say that no longer will Canada endorse 24 per cent as a rate of interest which we invite poor men to pay in this country.

subtopic: LIMITATIONS OF POWERS OF MONEY-LENDERS WITH RESPECT TO COST TO BORROWER, ETC.
speechtext:
I should like to say just a word in reply to the hon. member for Parry Sound. I thank him for his tribute to my sincerity, and I wish to pay a tribute to his.
I am sure that the views he has expressed are those which most people spontaneously express when they hear mentioned a rate such as 24 per cent per annum. But we have a large volume of evidence before us as to the effects of doing what he suggests, that is shutting off the general public from an opportunity of borrowing money at rates of interest such as these. The hon. gentleman said that if companies will not or cannot carry on business in this particular field unless they are permitted to charge rates of interest as high as this, the sooner we make it impossible for the public to pay these rates, the better for the public itself. He said that, he thought, spoke for itself.
Unfortunately that is not the way in which it works out. The universal experience, in other countries at least, has been that when companies are denied by law the right to charge rates of interest which will lead them to do business and, therefore, to invest their capital in the business, the general public is not prevented from borrowing money; the needy borrower, the man with a sick child or a sick wife, finds someone who will lend him some money, and unfortunately the man he finds who will lend him the money is usually lawless, is usually cunning, and charges him a rate of interest far in excess of the rate which strikes us all at first blush as being pretty high.
I read-and if the hon. gentleman has not read it I suggest he do so-the evidence on this point which was given before the banking and commerce committee, particularly the evidence of the representative of the Russell Sage foundation and other witnesses who gave expert testimony as to this business in the United States of America. Their evidence was substantially to this effect, that in those states which passed laws cutting down to one and a half or one per cent a month the rate which loan companies could charge, those companies, which they termed legitimate companies, left the state, they did not bother
with it, they did not carry on the business. The result was that a large volume of loans continued to be made, but the loans were made by loan sharks and the ordinary rate of interest was not two per cent a month but, in a great many of these cases, about twenty per cent a month. That was also the experience in other countries.
If we could put on a huge police force, possibly we could prevent anybody from borrowing money from anybody else at a high rate of interest. Even then, I am afraid, there would be some way of circumventing the law. That is the reason for the government's action. It is not because the government or anybody else likes the sound of two per cent a month or 24 per cent a year; it is because experience has shown that this is, not the ideal way but the only practical way, of preventing far worse abuses, terrible abuses, abuses that bring all sorts of misery in their train. That is why this legislation is being introduced.
The hon. gentleman made some reference to his constituency. He said that if these companies go into his constituency and start lending money at 24 per cent per annum abuses and evils will result. Well, these companies at the present time have the power to lend and are lending money at more than tiwo per cent a month; they are lending money at two and a half per cent a month. That is not the worst of it. All I can speak about with personal knowledge is the condition in my own constituency. There is in my constituency a loan company incorporated under the laws of Nova Scotia. I find that this company or one allied with it has been lending money in that province at an effective annual rate of 53-31 per cent. This is something that we have to meet. If we pass this legislation, in my constituency the rate is going to be cut down to two per cent a month, and that is going to happen all along the line to these forty-six companies which are incorporated by provincial jurisdictions from one end of the dominion to the other. The dominion-incorporated companies are not going to be allowed to charge as much as they are charging at the present time, and with a certain amount of what I think it is fair to call legitimate capital in the business, the general public, the people who have to have money, who feel that they have to have money, will not be driven up the alleyways and into the back offices of high buildings to cruel and ruthless exploiters who will charge them 50 and 100 and 1,000 per cent. I gave one instance here yesterday of 91,000 per cent. That is the reason for this legislation.

speechtext:
I realize that the
minister is having a difficult task because he is trying to make the best of a bad job. There is a principle at stake here, and we rise to protest more against the principle than to question the actual legality of the idea which the minister has in mind. The effect of shutting off the general public from borrowing at such rates would, I believe, be beneficial. We were brought up on this philosophy:
Neither a borrower nor a lender be;
For loan oft loses both itself and friend,
And borrowing dulls the edge of husbandry.
If we carried that principle into our later years we should be much better off. This country would have been much better off had that idea prevailed generally, and when we have before us a bill which proposes to reduce the rate of interest to a certain limited amount, that is a step in the right direction. There is no doubt about that. But the principle here is one of usury, and we are probably encouraging people to borrow money. As the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght) observed, we are encouraging them to borrow to their own downfall. I suggest, therefore, that constant vigilance is needed on the part of the government. Perhaps a few words of Edmund Burke would not be out of place here. He.was a great British statesman, who saw many injustices in the laws of the land, and in his day he said:
The question is not whether you have a right to render your people miserable, but whether it is not in your interest to make them happy.
It seems to me it is the right of the government if possible to make our people happy, and the only way in which we can make the people happy is to remove the causes of unhappiness. But the principle here is one that more or less backs up usury, something that we should like to get rid of.

If it meets that need, then I should think that, taking a larger risk, it might be entitled to a higher rate of interest.
