The full penalty will never be imposed. This bill may be all right for the lawyers, but I doubt if the minister will borrow any money under this legislation. Oh, no; he will not borrow money under this statute, but he will apply it to other people. I wonder if he has had any practical experience in connection with the enforcement of statutes of this kind. For many years I was chairman of a police commission; I saw many of these federal acts in the police court under Colonel Denison. He would not enforce them because they contained such loopholes and jokers as are in this section. A magistrate will construe an act according to the

text-book concerning the construction of statutes; that is, strictly and in accordance with the words of the section and the marginal notes. He will not link it to any interpretation act or any other part of the statute. It must be definite and exclusive; it cannot be made cumulative with any other penalties under the act.
In my opinion it is no wonder that we have over-government and over-taxation in this country with the way in which the departments go about their business. Each department has a law officer who passes upon the statutes concerning that department. Why, that law officer is over the Attorney General of Canada, who is the chief law officer of the crown. He is not here at the moment, but he would tell you that in practice he cannot give an opinion; it is against the rules for him to give a legal opinion in regard to any bill before the house or any committee of the house. The practice should be to have all bills of this kind passed upon by the Department of Justice. A statute of this kind may be declared ultra vires of this parliament by some magistrate. Mind you, a magistrate can declare an act ultra vires of parliament; so can a county court or a supreme court judge.
In my opinion there is more red tape about this statute than about the Bank Act or the Bills of Exchange Act, which are simple statutes, easily understood. The metaphysical language used in the bill and by the minister to-night may be all right for the shark loan companies and Shylocks, but it cannot be understood so clearly by the law courts. I do not wonder at the expenses of this country going up as they are when we have such overlapping and over-government, and when we have a responsible minister of the crown coming here and introducing a bill like this, which has not received the stamp of approval of the chief law officer of the crown.

This particular bill, in my opinion enables the government of the day to have this matter spread on all the fences and billboards. They will have the money lenders all in a rowboat-just as they had the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe). It will be in the rowboat, and it will be said that the Minister of National Revenue under this bill has all the Shylocks under control. These people operate secretly. They hold in utmost contempt any statutes passed by provinces or by the parliament of Canada. I asked a question in the house the other day, and received a return from the Department of Justice to the effect that they had no information about any transaction, and that they knew of nobody enforcing the Alien Labour Act. Then I asked the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar), and received the same answer: "No information," although it is his duty to act.

Mr. Speaker, like so many other members, while this bill was under discussion I was in two minds whether to support or oppose it. I realize that the committees which considered it last year and this year gave the matter a great deal of thought, and I feel that the minister must have given much thought to the bill, so I should have liked to support it. Yet I believe that it is wrong to support a bill of this kind, carrying this exorbitant rate of interest, even though the rate of two per cent a month includes something besides interest. Surely this government can produce a better measure than the present bill. I am almost convinced that we are not conferring a favour upon people who have to resort to borrowing of this kind, by making the opportunity available to them, because we are binding them forever to payment of usury. Also it seems to me, in view of the barrage of propaganda to which hon. members have been exposed since this measure came forward, that the lenders regard it as very good legislation from their point of view, or they would not be so anxious to see it passed. I also had my mind influenced against the bill by what was said by the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens), the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght) and a number of others.
I do not believe that we should at this time pass this measure. If the government cannot devise a better method of protection for people of small means, who are the people who would borrow under this bill, I do not think they are capable of doing very much for the people of Canada.
I therefore move, seconded by Mr. Coldwell:
That this bill be not now read a third time but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole with instructions that they have
power to amend it so that the "cost" of a loan as defined by clause (a) of section 2, shall not exceed one per centum per month on a loan for a period of fifteen months and one-half of one per centum per month for a loan for a greater period than fifteen months.

It has been tried repeatedly in various states of the union. Evidence covering the experience of these trials was given fully by experts before the banking and commerce committee. The result in all jurisdictions without exception has been that as the result of legislation of this kind, loans at twenty per cent a month have taken the place of loans at two and three per cent a month. For that reason I cannot accept the amendment. I believe it would inflict a great blow on the Canadian people. It may sound better to say one per cent a month instead of two per cent a month, but it would be a ruinous thing in the interests of the people to adopt an amendment of this kind at this stage. I believe, and I think everyone who has made a study of the matter is satisfied of the same thing, that if we adopt this amendment we shall not meet the problem at all; we shall be simply scuttling and sinking all this legislation. I want to make this point clear. It has been my position in this house for years and years. I can go back to the first session when I was in the house, when I sought an amendment to the Money Lenders Act.
Small Loans

That is twenty-eight years ago, and from that day to this I have fought this sort of business, and I have always contended that there was one way to control it, namely through the Money Lenders Act and through the criminal code. At this session-and I give the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) commendation for his action'-an appropriate amendment to the code will be brought down. That is the way in which you will control your money sharks

there, and there only. It is a grave question whether under this legislation you can control the money sharks at all. Personally I do not think you can. But you will control them through the criminal code. Therefore, when the minister says that if hon. members do not enact this legislation they will throw things wide open and increase distress, all you have to do is to go on with the amendment to the criminal code and apply the penalties therein set forth to anyone who charges these exorbitant rates of interest.
I invite the Minister of Justice to consider this point. As regards the section of this bill whereby we change costs and fees into interest by merely calling them costs and not interest, I question whether it will stand up in the courts, because I do not think this parliament can say that a charge to inspect a chattel mortgage, or a fee for this, that and the other, can be called interest. I do not believe that you can change by legislation the meaning of a term. Under the British North America Act we can legislate only in connection with interest unless through the criminal code we make a given set of actions criminal. That we are proposing in another bill to do. Give us this amendment to the criminal code; give us the present Money Lenders Act, and we shall then have power to correct these abuses -all of them, I do not care what they are- without thinking ever again of this bill. I would bring every one of these companies, from the so-called A class down to the most disreputable money lender, under the jurisdiction and control of the criminal code and the Money Lenders Act. I deprecate, therefore, the insistence of the minister that if we vote against this bill we are going to perpetrate some sort of ruin and desolation upon small borrowers in Canada. This will not happen if we proceed with the criminal code amendment; it will not affect the situation one iota. I will, therefore, support the amendment just offered because I am convinced that through this amendment to the criminal code and through that source only can we meet the terrible evil which is now abroad in the land.

It is quite obvious that the easiest thing for us to

do would be to throw up our hands in holy horror at 26 per cent and say that we shall have nothing to do with it. But one thing that has not been called to the attention of the house is this. We have already three loan companies operating under dominion charter, authorized to charge up to 2} per cent a month, and if we fail to-night to carry this bill into law, what will happen? I have not the evidence before me and I can speak only from memory, but other members of the committee will put me right if my recollection is at fault. I believe there is evidence adduced before the committee that this reduction in interest rate which we are making by this bill will mean the saving of something over $40,000 in one year to borrowers from one existing company. That is a distinct advantage in itself and a move in the right direction.
I am not in favour of high interest rates; far from it. But unless we leave some reputable companies in the field, then the work will be carried on by the so-called loan sharks; and from the evidence given to the committee it has been established to my satisfaction that two per cent is perhaps as low a rate as these legitimate companies can operate under. Every safeguard is set up under the Loan Companies Act to ensure that these companies cannot water their stock, cannot plough back profits, cannot issue bonus stock. We have a complete record of their earnings, and if in future years it is found that they are making more than a legitimate profit, then I am sure that every member of the house will unite in lowering the rate. It does seem to me, however, that for the sake of the poor unfortunates who need to borrow small sums of money we should maintain the legitimate companies in the field from whom these people can secure their requirements.
I think this country is deeply indebted to Mr. Finlayson for the long fight he has carried on for this reduction which will be put into effect if this measure passes. From questions asked from time to time this evening, I gather that hon. members do not fully realize the rates that are being charged. I take the $100 loan as an example. This rate of two per cent a month, figured out on a monthly retirement of an equal amount each month over fifteen months, would mean that the borrower would pay just over $16 as an overall charge of all costs including interest, legal charge for drawing up the chattel mortgage, legal charge for official registration of chattel mortgage, the expense of the company in sending out fifteen notices of monthly payments as and when they come due, expense of receiving fifteen payments and issuing receipts, setting

For the reasons I have given I am going to support the bill.

Mr. Speaker, there have been several points of view expressed on this bill to-night. I indicated last night that I was going to oppose the bill. I have said nothing to-night, but I propose to support the amendment for several reasons. In the first place I do not agree with those who feel that we should make it difficult for needy people to borrow. There are so many times in the life of any man when he needs money, and needs it sorely, especially in our cities-and under present conditions it is rapidly coming to be the case throughout the country-that I am not in favour of the point of view which seemed to be expressed by the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght) that we should make it difficult for these people to borrow. My feeling is that we should make it easier for them to borrow. There are those who will say immediately, "That is weakening the morale and economic fibre of t'he people." Well, Mr. Speaker, it is a fundamental truth that there is a condition developing in our society which must be met by adjustments different from any we have known previously. This insistent demand for small loans is another evidence that there is a decrease in the purchasing power in the hands of the people which simply must be met. Any light treatment of this condition certainly will not remove this condition.
That being so, I am going to point out several factors which I believe have a bearing on this situation. I am told that the losses sustained by the loan companies amount to less than one per cent of the money loaned; I am speaking entirely from memory. This would indicate that the people who borrow money under these circumstances are honest people who intend to pay back and who do pay back the money they borrow. Certainly we ought to be ready to favour people like that. I was interested in the remark of the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Spence) a short time ago, to the effect that not so many years ago the bankers of the needy were the butcher, the baker and the grocer of the community, and he deprecated the fact that those small businesses were being forced out of existence by the development of large organizations such as the chain stores. This makes it so much more important that we should make available to the people who are suffering loans at low rates of interest. But if the ordinary grocer in the community could carry the needy people of that community for six or eight months I am utterly unable to see why the people of the whole dominion cannot be so organized that they can become the banker for the needy people
of the country. Many a time the small grocer charged no interest at all on his overdue accounts; and many a time those who were able to pay were charged just a little extra in order to make up his loss-those of us who are familiar with the way in which the small country or community grocer carried on understand this very well. So I utterly fail to see why the people of this dominion cannot manage to carry those who are in necessitous circumstances.
That may sound strange, but in future we shall have many things that may sound a good deal stranger. I feel that those who suggested that the banks of this country should be called upon to make loans to needy people were on sound ground. When we refer this bill back to the committee I am not going to require that we should pass a law to enable any loan company to grant these loans. It might be wise for the government to reorganize the whole set-up and see to it that the banks attend to the matter right away. So far as I can see, there is no reason why within three months we could not have the banks of this country making these loans, as the Canadian Bank of Commerce is doing to-day. Our banking institutions are already there; they have their equipment, personnel and organization. These small loan companies are merely duplicating the services the banks are already amply equipped to render. and I feel that we should call upon the banks to do their duty.
So, Mr. Speaker, for the reasons I have indicated, as well as for other reasons, I am going to support the amendment.
